name: Four Functions Approach (POLC Framework)
description: The first way to look at what managers do: four functions that run in a cycle around achieving the organization's stated purpose. The slide sets it beside Henri Fayol's POCCC.

parts.name: Planning
parts.text: Defining goals, setting the strategy and developing subplans to coordinate activities.

parts.name: Organizing
parts.text: Deciding what needs to be done, how it will be done and who is to do it.

parts.name: Leading
parts.text: Directing and coordinating the work activities of the organization's people.

parts.name: Controlling
parts.text: Monitoring activities to make sure they are done as planned.

name: Managerial Roles (Henry Mintzberg)
description: The management roles approach: Henry Mintzberg groups what managers do into ten roles under three headings.

parts.name: Interpersonal roles
parts.text: Figurehead, leader and liaison.

parts.name: Informational roles
parts.text: Monitor, disseminator and spokesperson.

parts.name: Decisional roles
parts.text: Entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator.

name: Skills and Competencies (Robert Katz and others)
description: The third way to look at a manager's job asks what skills managers need. The slide shows four.

parts.name: Conceptual skills
parts.text: Analyze and diagnose.

parts.name: Interpersonal skills
parts.text: Working well with others.

parts.name: Technical skills
parts.text: Possessing expert job knowledge.

parts.name: Political skills
parts.text: Political adeptness.

name: Management Levels
description: A pyramid of the levels of managers in an organization, from the top down.

parts.name: Top managers
parts.text: The top of the pyramid.

parts.name: Middle managers
parts.text: The second level.

parts.name: First-line managers
parts.text: The third level.

parts.name: Team leaders
parts.text: The base of the pyramid.

name: Efficiency and Effectiveness
description: Management is getting things done effectively and efficiently, with and through people. Efficiency is about the means (resource usage) and effectiveness is about the ends (goal attainment).

parts.name: Efficiency
parts.text: Doing things right: the means, resource usage with low waste.

parts.name: Effectiveness
parts.text: Doing the right things: the ends, goal attainment at a high level.

name: Three Characteristics of Organizations
description: An organization is a deliberate arrangement of people brought together to accomplish a specific purpose. The slide names three characteristics.

name: Three Levels of Influence (Layers of OB)
description: OB examines behavior at three rising levels: the individual, the group and the organization, with each step building on the one below.

parts.name: The individual
parts.text: Emotions, values and attitudes, perception and personality. Motivating self and others bridges to the group level.

parts.name: The group
parts.text: Negotiation, conflict, communication, and groups and teams. Power and politics bridges to the organization level.

parts.name: The organization
parts.text: Change, organizational culture, decision making and leadership.

name: A Framework for Studying Organizational Behavior
description: Three linked areas, joined by two-way arrows, that together make up the study of organizational behavior.

parts.name: Individual level
parts.text: Individual differences, mental ability and personality; learning, perception, attitudes, values and ethics; individual decision making and creativity; foundation concepts of motivation; conflict, stress and well-being.

parts.name: Groups and interpersonal relations
parts.text: Interpersonal communication; group dynamics and teamwork; leadership; power, politics and influence.

parts.name: The organizational system and the global environment
parts.text: Organizational structure and design; organizational culture and change; the learning organization and knowledge management; cultural diversity and international organizational behavior.

name: Contributing Disciplines to the OB Field
description: Four disciplines feed the OB field, which looks at behavior at a micro level (the individual) and a macro level (groups and organizations).

parts.name: Micro level
parts.text: The individual.

parts.name: Macro level
parts.text: Groups and organizations.

parts.name: Disciplines
parts.text: Psychology, social psychology, sociology and anthropology, shown from the top to the bottom of a triangle.

name: A Basic OB Model
description: Inputs lead to processes, which lead to outcomes, each at the individual, group and organizational level. An arrow loops from outcomes back to inputs.

parts.name: Inputs
parts.text: Individual level: diversity, personality, values. Group level: group structure, group roles, team responsibilities. Organizational level: structure, culture.

parts.name: Processes
parts.text: Individual level: emotions and moods, motivation, perception, decision making. Group level: communication, leadership, power and politics, conflict and negotiation. Organizational level: human resource management, change practices.

parts.name: Outcomes
parts.text: Individual level: attitudes and stress, task performance, citizenship behavior, withdrawal behavior. Group level: group cohesion, group functioning. Organizational level: productivity, survival.

name: Challenges Facing the Workplace
description: Challenges that press on the workplace from three levels.

parts.name: Organizational level
parts.text: Productivity, developing effective employees, global competition, managing in the global village.

parts.name: Group level
parts.text: Working with others, workforce diversity.

parts.name: Individual level
parts.text: Job satisfaction, empowerment, behaving ethically.

name: The Marketing Process
description: The four steps that make up the marketing process.

parts.name: Analyzing marketing opportunities
parts.text: Step 1.

parts.name: Selecting target markets
parts.text: Step 2.

parts.name: Developing the marketing mix
parts.text: Step 3.

parts.name: Managing the marketing effort
parts.text: Step 4.

name: Create Value for Customers, Capture Value from Customers in Return
description: A five-box model of marketing. The first four boxes create value for customers and build customer relationships; the fifth captures value from customers in return.

parts.name: Understand the marketplace
parts.text: Understand the market place and customer needs and wants.

parts.name: Construct an integrated marketing program
parts.text: A program that delivers superior value.

parts.name: Build profitable relationships
parts.text: Build profitable relationships and create customer delight.

parts.name: Capture value from customers
parts.text: Capture value to create profits and customer equity.

name: Markets: Industry and Market
description: A simple picture of how sellers (the industry) and buyers (the market) are linked by four flows.

parts.name: Industry
parts.text: A collection of sellers.

parts.name: Market
parts.text: A collection of buyers: the set of actual and potential buyers of a product.

parts.name: From industry to market
parts.text: Communication, and goods or services.

parts.name: From market to industry
parts.text: Money, and information.

name: Key Customer Markets
description: The four key kinds of customer market.

name: Consumer Vs Industrial Marketing
description: A side-by-side comparison of marketing to individuals and households with marketing to organizations.

parts.name: Products
parts.text: Consumer: standardized and mass marketed. Industrial: niche specific.

parts.name: Purpose of purchase
parts.text: Consumer: personal consumption. Industrial: production of other goods and services.

parts.name: Market structure
parts.text: Consumer: geographically dispersed. Industrial: geographically concentrated.

parts.name: Demand
parts.text: Consumer: direct demand. Industrial: derived demand.

parts.name: Promotion
parts.text: Consumer: emphasis on advertising. Industrial: emphasis on personal selling.

name: Needs, Wants and Demands
description: A three-step chain: a basic need takes the form of a want, and a want backed by buying power becomes a demand.

parts.name: Needs
parts.text: Basic human requirements like food, security, clothing and survival.

parts.name: Wants
parts.text: The form needs take as they are shaped by culture and individual personality.

parts.name: Demands
parts.text: Wants backed by an ability to pay, that is, buying power.

name: Marketing Philosophies and Orientation
description: Five concepts a firm can use to guide its marketing, shown on the slide as five circles around marketing concepts.

parts.name: The production concept
parts.text: Focuses on the firm's internal capabilities and assumes consumers prefer products that are inexpensive and widely available. Strategy: production efficiency.

parts.name: The product concept
parts.text: Holds that consumers favour products that offer the most in quality, performance and features. Strategy: continuous product improvements.

parts.name: The selling concept
parts.text: Holds that people will buy more if aggressive sales techniques are used. Strategy: aggressive selling of the products the firm makes.

parts.name: The marketing concept
parts.text: Holds that achieving organizational goals depends on knowing the needs and wants of target markets. Strategy: finding the right product for the customer.

parts.name: The societal marketing concept
parts.text: Makes marketing decisions by weighing consumers' wants, the company's requirements, consumers' long term interests and society's long run interest.

name: The Selling Concept vs The Marketing Concept
description: Two arrows compare where each concept starts, what it focuses on, the means it uses and the ends it seeks.

parts.name: The selling concept
parts.text: Starting point: factory. Focus: existing products. Means: selling and promoting. Ends: profits through sales volume.

parts.name: The marketing concept
parts.text: Starting point: market. Focus: customer needs. Means: integrated marketing. Ends: profits through customer satisfaction.

name: Marketing and Selling Orientations
description: A table comparing the selling and the marketing orientation by focus, means and ends.

parts.name: Selling
parts.text: Focus: product. Means: aggressive selling and sales promotion, with emphasis on price variations to close the sale. Ends: maximise profits through sales maximisation.

parts.name: Marketing
parts.text: Focus: customer. Means: an integrated marketing plan covering product, price, promotion and distribution, backed by environmental scanning, consumer research and opportunity analysis. Ends: maximise profits through increased consumer satisfaction, and so raise market share.

name: Societal Marketing Concept Considerations
description: A triangle of the three things the societal marketing concept balances.

parts.name: Society
parts.text: Human welfare.

parts.name: Consumers
parts.text: Want satisfaction.

parts.name: Company
parts.text: Profits.

name: Holistic Marketing Concept
description: Holistic marketing sits at the centre of four linked parts. The slide does not explain the parts further.

name: What Can Be Marketed
description: The kinds of offerings the slides say can be marketed.

parts.name: Goods
parts.text: Cars, furniture, TV, refrigerators, machines, fresh food, canned food.

parts.name: Services
parts.text: Hotels, airlines, banking, consulting, renting.

parts.name: Events
parts.text: Trade shows, exhibitions, sporting events, local time-based markets.

parts.name: Persons
parts.text: Artists, musicians, athletes, CEO's, lawyers, financiers.

parts.name: Places
parts.text: Cities, states, regions, nation.

name: Marketing Mix (4 P's of Marketing)
description: Introduced by Jerome McCarthy in the 1960s, the marketing mix is a set of controllable variables, a toolkit to meet the needs of target customers and achieve the marketing objective.

parts.name: Product
parts.text: Product variety, quality, design, features, brand name, packaging, sizes, services, warranties, returns.

parts.name: Price
parts.text: List price, discounts, allowances, payment period, credit terms.

parts.name: Place
parts.text: Channels, coverage, assortments, locations, inventory, transport.

parts.name: Promotion
parts.text: Sales promotion, advertising, sales force, public relations, direct marketing.

parts.name: People, physical environment and process
parts.text: Three more elements shown in the seven-element marketing mix picture.

name: Marketing Environment
description: The actors and forces outside marketing that affect its ability to build and keep successful relationships with target customers. It splits into a micro and a macro environment.

parts.name: Micro environment
parts.text: Actors close to the company that directly affect its ability to serve its customers.

parts.name: Macro environment
parts.text: Larger societal forces outside the organization that affect it.

name: Micro Environment
description: Six actors close to the company, each linked to marketing by a two-way arrow.

parts.name: The company
parts.text: Internal groups such as top management, finance, research and development, purchasing, operations and accounting.

parts.name: Suppliers
parts.text: Provide the resources the company needs to produce its goods and services; an important link in the customer value delivery network.

parts.name: Marketing intermediaries
parts.text: Firms that help the company promote, sell and distribute its goods: retailers, logistics firms, marketing services agencies and financial intermediaries.

parts.name: Competitors
parts.text: A company must provide greater customer value and satisfaction than its competitors do.

parts.name: Publics
parts.text: Any group with an actual or potential interest in, or impact on, the organization's ability to achieve its objectives, such as media, the local public, labour unions, consumer organizations and environmental groups.

name: Macro Environment
description: Six larger societal forces around the company, each linked to it by a two-way arrow.

parts.name: Demographic forces
parts.text: The study of human populations by size, density, location, age, gender, diversity, race, occupation and other statistics.

parts.name: Economic forces
parts.text: Factors that affect consumer purchasing power and spending patterns, such as inflation, interest rates, employment and GDP.

parts.name: Natural forces
parts.text: Natural resources needed as inputs by marketers or affected by marketing activities.

parts.name: Technological forces
parts.text: Forces that create new technologies, creating new product and market opportunities.

parts.name: Political forces
parts.text: Laws, government agencies and pressure groups that influence or limit organizations and individuals.

parts.name: Cultural forces
parts.text: Society's basic values, perceptions, preferences, norms and behaviors.

name: PESTEL
description: A graphic of six letters, each standing for one force in the environment.

name: SWOT Analysis
description: A two by two grid for analyzing the marketing environment: internal against external factors, and positive against negative ones.

parts.name: Strengths
parts.text: Internal and positive: capabilities that may help the company reach its objectives.

parts.name: Weaknesses
parts.text: Internal and negative: limitations that may interfere with the company's ability to achieve its objectives.

parts.name: Opportunities
parts.text: External and positive: factors the company may be able to exploit to its advantage.

parts.name: Threats
parts.text: External and negative: current and emerging factors that may challenge the company's performance.

name: Types of AI: ANI, AGI and ASI
description: AI is grouped into three types by how far its intelligence reaches: narrow, general and super.

parts.name: ANI (Narrow AI, the Weak AI)
parts.text: Task-specific: built for a single function or a limited range of functions, and cannot learn beyond what it is programmed for. This is the AI in use today.

parts.name: AGI (General AI, the Strong AI)
parts.text: Machines that can think, reason, learn and adapt like a human across different domains. Still being developed.

parts.name: ASI (Super AI, the Future AI)
parts.text: Hypothetical AI that surpasses human intelligence in every way. It has not been achieved.

name: Difference between AI, ML and Deep Learning
description: Three nested circles: AI is the broadest field, machine learning sits inside it, and deep learning sits inside machine learning.

parts.name: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
parts.text: The broadest field: simulates human intelligence, from rule-based systems to learning algorithms.

parts.name: Machine Learning (ML)
parts.text: A subset of AI that enables systems to learn from data.

parts.name: Deep Learning (DL)
parts.text: A subset of ML that uses neural networks to mimic the human brain.

name: Core Capabilities of AI
description: Five capabilities against which AI systems are generally evaluated. A manager can use them as a checklist: which capability is a system actually showing?

parts.name: Learning
parts.text: Adapting behaviour based on data and experience.

parts.name: Reasoning
parts.text: Drawing conclusions from available information.

parts.name: Perception
parts.text: Interpreting sensory input such as images, sounds or text.

parts.name: Language understanding
parts.text: Communicating in human languages (natural language processing).

parts.name: Decision-making
parts.text: Choosing actions based on goals and context.

name: A Ladder of AI Proficiency
description: AI education is organised into three tiers, from general literacy through hands-on model building to advanced engineering. This course is built for the Basic tier and the early part of the Intermediate tier.

parts.name: Basic (AI literacy)
parts.text: For people with a non-technical background: what AI is and where it is used, core concepts such as data, algorithms, models, bias and ethics, and everyday tools. It asks: what is this and where is it used?

parts.name: Intermediate (builder or practitioner)
parts.text: For those who build or deploy simple models: data cleaning, supervised vs unsupervised learning, model training, validation and testing. It asks: how would I build or evaluate a simple version myself?

parts.name: Advanced (developer or researcher)
parts.text: For aspiring AI engineers and researchers: deep learning architectures, model optimisation, deployment and MLOps. It asks: how would I optimise, scale or deploy this?

name: Definitions of AI Across Eras
description: How the definition of AI has shifted, from building machines that mimic intelligent behaviour to building agents that achieve goals.

parts.name: John McCarthy (1956)
parts.text: The science and engineering of making intelligent machines.

parts.name: Classical or textbook definition
parts.text: Making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs, that mimic human intelligence by reasoning, learning, solving problems, understanding language and perceiving.

parts.name: Modern view (Russell and Norvig)
parts.text: The study of agents that perceive their environment and take actions that maximize their chances of achieving their goals.

name: The Five Eras of AI
description: A framework that organises AI's history into five eras, each defined by one question the field was trying to answer.

parts.name: Thinking about intelligence (1950s to 1960s)
parts.text: Can machines think? Alan Turing lays the foundation of machine intelligence and proposes a test for it.

parts.name: Rule-based conversation (1960s to 1970s)
parts.text: Can a machine hold a conversation? Chatbots such as ELIZA and PARRY follow predefined rules.

parts.name: Knowledge and learning (1980s to 2000s)
parts.text: Can machines reason and learn from data? Expert systems and early machine learning.

parts.name: Deep learning (2012 onwards)
parts.text: Can machines perceive the world the way humans do? Neural networks break through in vision, speech and language.

parts.name: Generative AI (2022 onwards)
parts.text: Can machines create and reason like a knowledgeable collaborator? Large language models.

name: AI Winters & Recoveries
description: Both AI winters followed the same pattern: limited expectations and a lack of computing power gave disappointing results, which led to reduced funding. Recovery came only with a genuine technical unlock.

parts.name: 1st AI winter (mid-1970s to mid-1980s)
parts.text: Rule-based systems failed to deliver on early promises and hardware could not meet AI's needs, so funding was cut, especially in the US and UK.

parts.name: 2nd AI winter (late 1980s to early 1990s)
parts.text: Commercial expert systems were costly to maintain, the market was saturated with vendors overselling, and Japan's Fifth Generation project fell short, so business and the public lost faith.

parts.name: The cycle
parts.text: Limited expectations and a lack of computing power, then disappointing results, then reduced funding, then recovery.

name: The AI Comeback: Big Data + GPUs + Deep Learning
description: AI's comeback around 2012 came from three enablers converging at once. Each was needed and none was enough on its own.

parts.name: Big Data (the fuel)
parts.text: Pioneers: Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat (Google). Gave AI the raw material to learn.

parts.name: GPUs (the powerhouse)
parts.text: Pioneer: Ian Buck (NVIDIA), who developed CUDA. Made AI training fast and scalable.

parts.name: Deep Learning (the brain)
parts.text: Pioneers: Hinton, LeCun and Bengio. Created models that could learn deeply from data.

name: The Chatbot Lineage
description: Five conversational systems, each more convincing than the last, built on rule-based foundations until Cleverbot began learning from conversation data.

parts.name: ELIZA (1966)
parts.text: Simulated a psychotherapist with keyword pattern matching; no memory, reasoning or learning.

parts.name: PARRY (1972)
parts.text: Added internal beliefs and emotional states to simulate a patient.

parts.name: Catherine (1991)
parts.text: Larger knowledge bases, better dialogue management and more natural conversation.

parts.name: Eugene Goostman
parts.text: Designed as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy so its mistakes seemed natural; its 2014 claim to pass the Turing Test is disputed.

parts.name: Cleverbot (2011)
parts.text: Learned from millions of past conversations instead of fixed rules: a shift toward data-driven AI.

name: Modern AI Milestones: Watson, AlphaGo, GPTs
description: Three systems that trace AI's move from narrow question answering, to strategic intuition, to general-purpose language.

parts.name: IBM Watson (2011)
parts.text: Question answering, using NLP and information retrieval.

parts.name: AlphaGo (2016)
parts.text: Strategic thinking, using deep reinforcement learning and tree search to master an intuition-driven game.

parts.name: GPTs (2018 to present)
parts.text: Language understanding and generation, using transformers and large language models.

name: How AGI Works
description: Six abilities arranged around a robot head that together describe how AGI is meant to work.

parts.name: General learning
parts.text: Learns from experience and adapts to new tasks.

parts.name: Natural language understanding
parts.text: Deeply comprehends and uses human language.

parts.name: Self-improvement
parts.text: Enhances its own abilities over time.

parts.name: Memory integration
parts.text: Stores and recalls information effectively.

parts.name: Autonomous goal setting
parts.text: Sets goals and makes independent decisions.

parts.name: Common sense
parts.text: Understands and reasons about everyday knowledge.

name: Six Principles for Defining AGI
description: Six principles the research article proposes for defining AGI.

parts.name: Capabilities, not processes
parts.text: Focus on what a system can do and ignore consciousness.

parts.name: Generality and performance
parts.text: Evaluate the two separately.

parts.name: Cognitive and metacognitive tasks
parts.text: Prioritize these, not robotics.

parts.name: Ecological validity
parts.text: Real-world relevance.

parts.name: Levels, not an endpoint
parts.text: Define progress as levels rather than a single endpoint.

name: Levels of AGI: The Framework
description: A matrix of performance levels against generality (narrow vs general). AGI is reached when many tasks are done competently across a range of domains, not when one task is done superhumanly.

parts.name: Level 0: No AI
parts.text: For example, calculators.

parts.name: Level 1: Emerging AGI
parts.text: For example, ChatGPT.

parts.name: Level 2: Competent AGI
parts.text: Not yet achieved.

parts.name: Level 5: ASI
parts.text: Artificial Superintelligence.

name: Levels of Autonomy
description: Ways people and AI can work together, from AI as a simple tool to a fully autonomous agent. Higher AGI plus higher autonomy means higher risk.

parts.name: Tool
parts.text: Basic automation, such as a grammar checker.

parts.name: Consultant
parts.text: AI gives advice when prompted.

parts.name: Collaborator
parts.text: Shared goals and interactive learning.

parts.name: Expert
parts.text: AI leads and the human gives feedback.

parts.name: Agent
parts.text: Fully autonomous AI.

name: COSO Framework
description: The five components of internal control. With AI, each component can be improved through better risk prediction, real-time monitoring, data-driven decisions and automated controls.

name: AI in Internal Control: Theoretical Frameworks
description: Three theoretical frameworks for understanding the role of AI in internal control.

parts.name: Resource-Based View (RBV)
parts.text: AI is a strategic resource that adds VRIN qualities (value, rarity, inimitability, non-substitutability) and gives a competitive edge.

parts.name: Task-Technology Fit (TTF)
parts.text: AI is effective when the technology matches what the task needs.

parts.name: COSO framework enhancement with AI
parts.text: AI improves all five COSO components.

name: Task-Technology Fit Matrix (Figure 6)
description: A matrix rating how well five AI technologies fit five internal control tasks as High, Medium or Low.

parts.name: Risk assessment
parts.text: High for ML, data analytics and anomaly detection; medium for NLP and RPA.

parts.name: Auditing
parts.text: High for ML, NLP and data analytics; medium for RPA and anomaly detection.

parts.name: Transaction monitoring
parts.text: High for ML, RPA, data analytics and anomaly detection; low for NLP, the only low cell.

parts.name: Compliance checking
parts.text: High for NLP and RPA; medium for ML, data analytics and anomaly detection.

parts.name: Fraud detection
parts.text: High for ML and anomaly detection; medium for NLP, RPA and data analytics.

name: How Siri Works
description: Six steps a voice assistant follows, from hearing the wake word to learning from use.

parts.name: Voice input and wake word detection
parts.text: The microphone keeps listening for the wake word, Hey Siri.

parts.name: Speech recognition (ASR)
parts.text: Speech is converted into text.

parts.name: Natural language understanding (NLU)
parts.text: The text is analysed to find the intent and its parameters.

parts.name: Task management and query resolution
parts.text: The command is routed to the right domain-specific engine.

parts.name: Action execution
parts.text: A response is generated and the action is performed.

parts.name: Feedback loop and on-device learning
parts.text: Differential privacy is used to improve from aggregate interactions.

name: Core Characteristics of ASI
description: Five features of Artificial Superintelligence, a hypothetical AI that would surpass human intelligence in all domains.

parts.name: Cognitive superiority
parts.text: Solves complex problems faster and better than humans in all fields.

parts.name: Self-improving
parts.text: Can recursively upgrade its own algorithms and hardware.

parts.name: Goal-driven
parts.text: Works toward programmed or learned goals, which may or may not align with human values.

parts.name: Autonomous
parts.text: Makes independent decisions and acts without human input.

parts.name: Generalized knowledge
parts.text: Applies reasoning across disciplines such as science, economics and law.

name: Risks and Challenges of ASI
description: Four risks and challenges the slides raise about ASI, AI that would surpass human intelligence in all domains.

parts.name: Alignment problem
parts.text: Will ASI share human values? Misaligned goals could lead to catastrophic outcomes.

parts.name: Control problem
parts.text: Can we control something vastly more intelligent than us?

parts.name: Existential risk (X-Risk)
parts.text: ASI might harm humanity, by accident or on purpose, if misaligned or malicious.

parts.name: Concentration of power
parts.text: ASI controlled by a single corporation or government could lead to global inequality or totalitarianism.

name: How AI Keeps Learning (Figure 14)
description: A rising timeline of how AI systems keep learning and adapting to new business environments and challenges.

parts.name: Initial learning (2022)
parts.text: Basic models and small datasets; data collection and basic pattern recognition.

parts.name: Continuous learning (2023)
parts.text: Adapts using feedback, new data and real-time inputs.

parts.name: Advanced learning (2024)
parts.text: More complex algorithms and larger datasets improve decision accuracy and flexibility.

parts.name: Mature learning (2025)
parts.text: Built into real-time autonomous decision making and adapts to new challenges with minimal human intervention.

name: Evolution of AI Technologies (Figure 3)
description: A timeline of AI technologies from early AI to future concepts.

parts.name: AGI
parts.text: Predicted for the mid-21st century.

parts.name: ASI
parts.text: A hypothetical future.

parts.name: UBI
parts.text: Universal Basic Intelligence, a future concept.

name: Domains Covered by ANI
description: Nine domains in which narrow AI systems work.

name: AI in Marketing Management
description: Six areas of marketing where AI is applied, arranged around an AI head.

parts.name: Content creation
parts.text: AI writes blogs, ad copies and product descriptions.

parts.name: Customer engagement
parts.text: AI chatbots and assistants offer 24/7 support.

parts.name: Marketing automation
parts.text: Automates emails, SMS and campaigns.

parts.name: Predictive analytics
parts.text: Predicts future trends from data.

parts.name: Digital marketing
parts.text: Optimizes ad spend, targeting and A/B testing.

parts.name: Ads & targeting
parts.text: Delivers personalized ads to the right audience.

name: AI in HRM
description: Six areas of human resources management where AI is applied.

parts.name: Recruitment & hiring
parts.text: Automates resume screening and candidate matching.

parts.name: Onboarding
parts.text: Delivers personalized welcome kits, FAQs and training schedules.

parts.name: Employee training
parts.text: Uses AI tutors and adaptive learning platforms.

parts.name: Performance evaluation
parts.text: Tracks KPIs and gives unbiased feedback reports.

parts.name: Employee engagement
parts.text: Monitors sentiment, recommends wellness activities and uses AI chatbots for HR queries.

parts.name: Talent management
parts.text: Identifies high-potential employees and suggests career development paths.

name: AI in Accounting & Finance Management
description: Key functions in accounting and finance where AI is applied.

parts.name: Transaction coding
parts.text: Automates data entry and classification of expenses.

parts.name: Invoice processing
parts.text: Extracts data, verifies and processes bills faster.

parts.name: Expense reporting
parts.text: Tracks spending and flags anomalies.

parts.name: Financial analysis
parts.text: Forecasts trends, prepares dashboards and aids decision-making.

parts.name: Talent management
parts.text: Optimizes hiring for finance roles with predictive analytics.

parts.name: Risk assessment
parts.text: Evaluates financial risks and credit scores.

parts.name: Fraud detection
parts.text: Flags suspicious activity using AI pattern recognition.

name: AI in Operation Management and Supply Chain Management
description: Key roles of AI in operations and the supply chain.

parts.name: Demand forecasting
parts.text: Predicts future product demand using data trends.

parts.name: Inventory management
parts.text: Tracks stock levels and automates reordering.

parts.name: Quality control
parts.text: Detects product defects using AI vision systems.

parts.name: Predictive maintenance
parts.text: Prevents machine failures by forecasting maintenance needs.

parts.name: Supply chain optimization
parts.text: Improves logistics, reduces delays and cuts costs.

parts.name: Autonomous vehicles
parts.text: Enables driverless transport and smart deliveries.

name: The Accounting Equation
description: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Every transaction, however complex, keeps this equation in balance.

parts.name: Assets
parts.text: What the business owns: cash, inventory, equipment, buildings.

parts.name: Liabilities
parts.text: What the business owes: loans, accounts payable, unearned revenue.

parts.name: Equity
parts.text: The owner's residual claim: capital invested plus retained earnings.

name: The Five Elements of Financial Statements
description: Every financial statement item traces to one of five elements. Assets, liabilities and equity show financial position at a point in time; income and expenses show performance over a period.

parts.name: Asset
parts.text: A present economic resource the entity controls as a result of past events, with the potential to produce economic benefits.

parts.name: Liability
parts.text: A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events.

parts.name: Equity
parts.text: The residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting all its liabilities.

parts.name: Income
parts.text: Increases in assets, or decreases in liabilities, that increase equity, other than owner contributions. Includes revenues and gains.

parts.name: Expenses
parts.text: Decreases in assets, or increases in liabilities, that decrease equity, other than owner distributions. Includes expenses and losses.

name: Double-Entry Bookkeeping: Which Side Increases an Account?
description: Every transaction touches at least two accounts, and total debits always equal total credits. Memory tip: DEAD accounts (dividends, expenses, assets, draws) increase with debits; everything else increases with credits.

parts.name: Assets
parts.text: Debit increases, credit decreases.

parts.name: Expenses
parts.text: Debit increases, credit decreases.

parts.name: Liabilities
parts.text: Debit decreases, credit increases.

parts.name: Equity
parts.text: Debit decreases, credit increases.

parts.name: Revenue
parts.text: Debit decreases, credit increases.

name: The Three Core Financial Statements
description: Together they answer three questions: what do we own, how did we perform, and where did the cash go?

parts.name: Balance sheet
parts.text: A snapshot at one point in time. Assets = Liabilities + Equity. What do we own and owe today?

parts.name: Income statement
parts.text: Performance over a period. Revenue minus expenses = net income. Did we make a profit this year?

parts.name: Cash flow statement
parts.text: Cash movement over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities. Where did our cash actually go?

name: Accrual vs. Cash Basis Accounting
description: The difference is timing: when revenue and expenses are recorded.

parts.name: Cash basis
parts.text: Record revenue when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. Simple; used by small businesses and freelancers.

parts.name: Accrual basis
parts.text: Record revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash moves. Required under GAAP for most companies.

name: Key Financial Ratios
description: Four ratios that turn raw statement numbers into signals about liquidity, profitability and leverage.

parts.name: Current ratio
parts.text: Current assets ÷ current liabilities. Liquidity: can we cover short-term bills?

parts.name: Gross margin
parts.text: Gross profit ÷ revenue. Profitability: how efficient is production?

parts.name: Net margin
parts.text: Net income ÷ revenue. Profitability: what share of sales is profit?

parts.name: Debt-to-equity
parts.text: Total liabilities ÷ total equity. Leverage: how much financing is debt?

name: Core GAAP Principles
description: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles keep financial statements consistent and comparable. The slide lists six.

parts.name: Revenue recognition
parts.text: Recognize revenue when it is earned, not necessarily when cash is received.

parts.name: Matching principle
parts.text: Match expenses to the revenue they helped generate, in the same period.

parts.name: Consistency
parts.text: Use the same accounting methods period to period so results are comparable.

parts.name: Conservatism
parts.text: When in doubt, record losses early and gains only when they are realized.

parts.name: Going concern
parts.text: Assume the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.

parts.name: Materiality
parts.text: Only items large enough to influence a decision need precise, separate treatment.

name: Diagram 5.1: How Recognition Links the Elements of Financial Statements
description: Recognition captures an item that meets the definition of an element so it is included in the statements. The diagram shows how opening equity, the changes in equity during the period and closing equity fit together.

parts.name: Opening statement of financial position
parts.text: Assets minus liabilities equal equity at the beginning of the reporting period.

parts.name: Statement(s) of financial performance
parts.text: Income minus expenses.

parts.name: Contributions and distributions
parts.text: Contributions from holders of equity claims minus distributions to them. Together with income and expenses, these are the changes in equity.

parts.name: Closing statement of financial position
parts.text: Assets minus liabilities equal equity at the end of the reporting period.

name: The Three-Step Method for the Five Elements
description: The worked examples follow the same three steps to turn a list of accounts into a balanced accounting equation.

parts.name: Step 1: Accounting items
parts.text: List the accounts and their amounts.

parts.name: Step 2: Classification into the five elements
parts.text: Sort each item into assets, liabilities, equity, income or expenses, and total each group.

parts.name: Step 3: Verify the accounting equation
parts.text: Check that assets equal liabilities plus equity, with the net profit for the year added to equity.

name: Six Building Blocks of Financial Accounting
description: Six ideas that form one connected system, from the accounting equation to ratios and GAAP.

parts.name: The accounting equation
parts.text: Keeps every transaction in balance.

parts.name: Double-entry and debits/credits
parts.text: How that balance is recorded.

parts.name: The three financial statements
parts.text: Tell what you own, earned and collected.

parts.name: Accrual vs. cash basis
parts.text: Accrual accounting times revenue and expenses to when they occur.

parts.name: Depreciation
parts.text: Spreads asset cost over its useful life.

parts.name: Financial ratios and GAAP
parts.text: Turn the numbers into reliable, comparable insight.

name: Basic Principles of Economics
description: Six basic principles of economics listed on the slide.

parts.name: People are rational and rational people think at the margin

name: Role of a Manager
description: A manager directs resources to achieve a stated business goal. The slides list six parts of the role and then explain each one.

parts.name: Identify goals and constraints for the firm
parts.text: Well-defined goals lead to the right decisions; constraints come from scarcity.

parts.name: Understand the nature of profits
parts.text: Profits ensure survival, growth and returns to owners.

parts.name: Understand the role of incentives
parts.text: Design incentives that line up employees' interests with the firm's goals.

parts.name: Understand the nature of the market in which the firm operates
parts.text: Consumers, producers and governments all shape the market.

parts.name: Understand time value of money
parts.text: Business decisions are long horizon, and the value of money today differs from its value tomorrow.

parts.name: Ability to think at a margin
parts.text: Compare the additional benefit and additional cost of an action.

name: Accounting Profit vs Economic Profit
description: Two ways of measuring profit. The difference is whether opportunity costs are counted.

parts.name: Accounting profit
parts.text: Total revenue minus explicit costs. Used in financial statements; ignores opportunity costs.

parts.name: Economic profit
parts.text: Total revenue minus explicit and implicit costs. Used for managerial decision-making; includes opportunity costs.

name: Factors that Affect Profitability
description: Five sets of factors point at sustainable industry profits.

parts.name: Entry
parts.text: Entry costs, speed of adjustment, sunk costs, economies of scale, network effects, reputation, switching costs, government restraints.

parts.name: Power of input suppliers
parts.text: Supplier concentration, price and productivity of alternative inputs, relationship-specific investments, supplier switching costs, government restraints.

parts.name: Power of buyers
parts.text: Buyer concentration, price and value of substitute products or services, relationship-specific investments, customer switching costs, government restraints.

parts.name: Industry rivalry
parts.text: Concentration; price, quantity, quality or service competition; degree of differentiation; switching costs; timing of decisions; information; government restraints.

parts.name: Substitutes & complements
parts.text: Price and value of surrogate products or services, price and value of complementary products or services, network effects, government restraints.

name: Marginal Principle
description: Managers decide by comparing the additional benefit and the additional cost of one more unit of an action.

parts.name: Marginal benefit (MB)
parts.text: The additional benefit gained from one more unit of an action.

parts.name: Marginal cost (MC)
parts.text: The additional cost of one more unit of an action.

parts.name: Decision rule
parts.text: Take an action only if MB > MC. To maximize net benefits, increase the control variable up to the point where MB = MC.

parts.name: For output decisions
parts.text: Produce another unit if MR > MC and stop when MR = MC.

name: Discrete vs. Continuous Decisions
description: Managers make two types of decisions: tables are used for discrete decisions and calculus for continuous ones.

parts.name: Discrete decisions
parts.text: Choices are made in whole units, no calculus is needed and marginal values come from changes. Examples: hire one more worker, open another store.

parts.name: Continuous decisions
parts.text: Choices can take any value, calculus is used and marginal values come from derivatives. Examples: set the selling price, decide advertising expenditure.

name: Net Present Value Decision Rule
description: NPV is the sum of the present values of all future cash flows from a project, minus the initial cost.

parts.name: NPV > 0
parts.text: Accept the project.

parts.name: NPV < 0
parts.text: Reject the project.

name: Various Kinds of Utility
description: Value is not only created in the factory. It is also created by moving things (place) and by timing when they are available (time).

parts.name: Form utility
parts.text: The form in which a product is available, such as whole chicken, chicken parts or cooked chicken; each step adds value.

parts.name: Place utility
parts.text: Where a product is available: convenience, home delivery.

parts.name: Time utility
parts.text: When a product is available, for example when it is needed urgently.

name: Determinants of Demand and the Demand Function
description: Things other than the good's own price that move the whole demand curve, summed up in the demand function Qxd = f(Px, Py, M, H).

parts.name: Income (M)
parts.text: Normal good or inferior good.

parts.name: Prices of related goods (Py)
parts.text: Prices of substitutes and prices of complements.

parts.name: Other variables (H)
parts.text: Any other variable affecting demand.

name: Determinants of Supply and the Supply Function
description: Supply shifters, summed up in the supply function Qxs = f(Px, Pr, W, H).

parts.name: Input prices (W)
parts.text: For example, wages.

parts.name: Number of firms
parts.text: Entry and exit.

parts.name: Substitutes in production (Pr)
parts.text: The price of a production substitute.

parts.name: Taxes
parts.text: Excise tax and ad valorem tax.

parts.name: Other variables (H)
parts.text: Any other variable affecting supply.

name: Price Restrictions
description: Two kinds of legal limits on price and what each does to the market.

parts.name: Price ceiling
parts.text: The maximum legal price. Set below the equilibrium price, it causes a shortage, and consumers end up paying a full economic price above the ceiling.

parts.name: Price floor
parts.text: The minimum legal price. Set above the equilibrium price, it causes a surplus. Examples: minimum wage, agricultural price supports.

name: Comparative Static Analysis: Big Picture and Action Plan
description: A two-step way to use demand and supply analysis when an event hits a market.

parts.name: Step 1: Look for the big picture
parts.text: Work out how equilibrium price and quantity change when a determinant of supply or demand changes.

parts.name: Step 2: Organize an action plan
parts.text: Work out the needed changes in production, inventories, raw materials, human resources and marketing plans, and whether quantitative estimates are needed.

name: Suitability of Organization
description: The factors the group uses to choose an organization, with a rationale for the choice.

name: Statistical Approaches: Descriptive and Inferential
description: The two broad approaches in statistics.

parts.name: Descriptive statistics
parts.text: Methods for analysing, summarising and organising data, usually with graphs and numerical summaries. Example: a census.

parts.name: Inferential statistics
parts.text: Methods for drawing conclusions or making predictions about a population from a sample. Example: an exit poll.

name: Sample Versus Census
description: Conditions that favour using a sample or a full census.

parts.name: Budget
parts.text: Small favours a sample; large favours a census.

parts.name: Time available
parts.text: Short: sample. Long: census.

parts.name: Population size
parts.text: Large: sample. Small: census.

parts.name: Variance in the characteristic
parts.text: Small: sample. Large: census.

parts.name: Cost of sampling errors
parts.text: Low: sample. High: census.

parts.name: Nature of measurement
parts.text: Destructive: sample. Non-destructive: census.

parts.name: Attention to individual cases
parts.text: Yes: sample. No: census.

name: Steps in the Sampling Design Process
description: Five steps used to design a sample, shown through two real surveys.

parts.name: Target population
parts.text: Defined in terms of elements, sampling units, extent and time.

parts.name: Sampling frame
parts.text: The list or program used to reach the population, such as a computer program that generates random telephone numbers.

parts.name: Sampling technique
parts.text: For example, stratified sampling.

parts.name: Sample size
parts.text: How many respondents are surveyed.

parts.name: Execution
parts.text: Allocating the sample and selecting the respondents in practice.

name: Sampling Types: Probability and Non-Probability Sampling
description: In probability sampling every eligible individual has an equal chance of being selected; in non-probability sampling the researcher picks the sample by subjective judgment rather than at random.

parts.name: Simple random sampling
parts.text: Probability. Give every member a number and let a random number generator pick the sample.

parts.name: Systematic sampling
parts.text: Probability. Pick a random starting point, then every Nth member.

parts.name: Stratified sampling
parts.text: Probability. Divide the population into groups and select proportionate numbers at random from each.

parts.name: Cluster sampling
parts.text: Probability. Divide the data into clusters and randomly select whole clusters.

parts.name: Convenience sampling
parts.text: Non-probability. Select whoever is conveniently available.

parts.name: Consecutive sampling
parts.text: Non-probability. Sample one person or group, analyse it, then select more as needed.

parts.name: Quota sampling
parts.text: Non-probability. Pick individuals by specific traits so the sample reflects the population.

parts.name: Judgment or purposive sampling
parts.text: Non-probability. Selected using the researcher's knowledge or judgment.

parts.name: Snowball sampling
parts.text: Non-probability. Chain referral: members recommend further members.

name: Types of Data
description: A tree: data is either categorical (qualitative) or numerical (quantitative), and each branch splits in two.

parts.name: Nominal
parts.text: Categorical data with no order, such as gender, blood group or nationality.

parts.name: Ordinal
parts.text: Categorical data with an order, such as educational level or consumer satisfaction.

parts.name: Discrete
parts.text: Numerical data such as number of children, runs scored or size of the class.

parts.name: Continuous
parts.text: Numerical data such as height, weight or strike rate.

name: Scales of Measurement
description: Four scales, each adding a property to the one before it.

parts.name: Nominal
parts.text: Identity or category only. Example: gender.

parts.name: Ordinal
parts.text: Adds magnitude or rank, so the order of values is known. Example: doneness of meat.

parts.name: Interval
parts.text: Adds equal intervals, so values can be added and subtracted, but there is no true zero. Example: temperature in degrees.

parts.name: Ratio
parts.text: Adds an absolute (true) zero, so values can also be multiplied and divided. Example: age in years.

name: Scale Characteristics
description: Four characteristics that a measurement scale may have.

parts.name: Description
parts.text: Unique labels or descriptors that name each value of the scale.

parts.name: Order
parts.text: The relative sizes or positions of the descriptors.

parts.name: Distance
parts.text: Absolute differences between the scale descriptors are known.

parts.name: Origin
parts.text: The scale has a unique or fixed beginning, a true zero point.

name: Descriptive Statistics: Three Kinds of Measures
description: Measures computed from a sample are called sample statistics; computed from a population, they are population parameters.

name: Measures of Central Tendency
description: Five measures. Mean, median and mode give the central tendency score; percentiles and quartiles follow.

parts.name: Mean
parts.text: The average: the sum of the values divided by the number of values.

parts.name: Median
parts.text: The middle value that separates a data set into a higher and a lower half.

parts.name: Mode
parts.text: The value that appears most frequently in a data set.

name: Central Tendencies of Various Data Types
description: Which measures of central tendency fit each type of data.

parts.name: Nominal
parts.text: Mode only.

parts.name: Ordinal
parts.text: Mode and median.

parts.name: Discrete and continuous
parts.text: Mode, median and mean.

name: Quartiles
description: Three cut points that split ordered data into four parts, plus the interquartile range built from them.

parts.name: Q1
parts.text: 25% of the data lies between the minimum and Q1.

parts.name: Q2 (median)
parts.text: 50% of the data lies on each side.

parts.name: Q3
parts.text: 75% of the data lies between the minimum and Q3.

parts.name: Interquartile range (IQR)
parts.text: Q3 minus Q1: the spread of the middle 50% of the data, less affected by extreme values than the range.

name: Types of Probability
description: Three ways to arrive at a probability.

parts.name: Classical (theoretical)
parts.text: All outcomes equally likely, as with dice or coins.

parts.name: Empirical (relative frequency)
parts.text: Based on observations or experiments, such as late deliveries out of the last 100.

parts.name: Subjective
parts.text: Based on personal judgment or experience, such as a manager's estimate.

name: Probability Rules
description: The basic rules every probability follows.

parts.name: Rule 1
parts.text: Any probability lies between 0 and 1.

parts.name: Rule 2
parts.text: A certain event has probability 1.

parts.name: Rule 3
parts.text: The probability of the complement is 1 minus the probability of the event.

parts.name: Addition rule
parts.text: For 'or' events: if mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

parts.name: Multiplication rule
parts.text: For 'and' events: if independent, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

name: Mutually Exclusive, Independent and Exhaustive Events
description: Three ways events can relate to each other.

parts.name: Mutually exclusive
parts.text: Two events cannot happen at the same time, so P(A and B) = 0.

parts.name: Independent
parts.text: The occurrence of one does not affect the other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

parts.name: Mutually exhaustive
parts.text: At least one of the events must occur, covering all possible outcomes, so their combined probability is 1.

name: Probability Distribution Functions
description: The map of distributions covered in the module.

parts.name: Discrete distributions
parts.text: Bernoulli random variable, binomial distribution and Poisson distribution.

parts.name: Continuous distributions
parts.text: Uniform distribution, normal distribution and standard normal distribution (z).

name: Primary vs. Secondary Data
description: The two sources of data compared.

parts.name: Primary data
parts.text: Collected first-hand for a specific purpose, through surveys, experiments or interviews. Accurate and relevant, but costly and time-consuming.

parts.name: Secondary data
parts.text: Pre-existing data found in reports, articles and records. Cost-effective and accessible, but may lack fit or carry bias.

name: Data Collection Methods in Practice
description: Three ways to collect data.

parts.name: Observational
parts.text: Directly recording behaviors or phenomena.

parts.name: Survey-based
parts.text: Questionnaires and online forms for self-reported data.

parts.name: Experimental
parts.text: Manipulating variables to observe effects.

name: Designing a Data Collection Plan
description: Four steps to plan how data will be collected.

parts.name: Step 1
parts.text: Choose a research question.

parts.name: Step 2
parts.text: Decide on a primary, secondary or mixed approach.

parts.name: Step 3
parts.text: Draft the data collection procedure, such as a survey or experiment outline.

parts.name: Step 4
parts.text: Identify sources and plan how data will be recorded and stored.

name: Evaluation of Information Sources
description: Five factors on which an information source is evaluated.

parts.name: Purpose
parts.text: Why does the source exist? This shows the type and bias of the information.

parts.name: Authority
parts.text: What are the credentials of the authors or the sponsoring organisation?

parts.name: Scope
parts.text: How much information is there, is it selective or comprehensive, and how old is the data?

parts.name: Audience
parts.text: Whom does the source cater to, and what level of knowledge does it assume?

parts.name: Format
parts.text: How quickly can you find the information, and how easy is the source to access?

name: Scientific Business Researchers Operate at Two Levels
description: Research works at an abstract level and an empirical level.

parts.name: Abstract level
parts.text: Concepts and propositions: knowledge that exists only as an idea.

parts.name: Empirical level
parts.text: Variables and hypotheses: knowledge that can be verified by experience or observation.

name: Types of Hypotheses
description: A hypothesis is a proposition formulated for empirical testing. The slides name four types.

parts.name: Descriptive
parts.text: States the existence, size, form or distribution of some variable.

parts.name: Relational
parts.text: States a relationship between two variables with respect to some case.

parts.name: Correlational
parts.text: States that variables occur together in some specified manner, without implying causal direction.

parts.name: Causal
parts.text: Implies a cause-and-effect relationship between variables.

name: Functions of a Hypothesis
description: What a hypothesis does for a study.

parts.name: Direction
parts.text: It guides the direction of the study.

parts.name: Relevance
parts.text: It identifies which facts are relevant and which are not.

parts.name: Design
parts.text: It suggests which research design is most appropriate.

parts.name: Conclusions
parts.text: It provides a framework for organizing the conclusions.

name: Types of Research
description: The ways research can be classified.

parts.name: Exploratory vs descriptive vs analytical
parts.text: To gain familiarity; to describe the present state of affairs; to critically evaluate causation from available information.

parts.name: Fundamental vs applied
parts.text: To build on theory in a general area; for a specific application.

parts.name: Quantitative vs qualitative
parts.text: An objective assessment based on measurement of quantity; a subjective assessment of emotions, opinions and behaviours.

parts.name: Conceptual vs empirical vs simulation
parts.text: Based on abstract theory; based on experience or observation; based on observations in an artificial environment.

parts.name: In terms of time
parts.text: One-time research or longitudinal research.

parts.name: In terms of location
parts.text: Library, laboratory or field research.

parts.name: In terms of outcome
parts.text: Conclusion-oriented or decision-oriented research.

name: Types of Variables
description: The kinds of variables a study can include.

parts.name: Independent
parts.text: The variable that comes before, and affects, the dependent variable.

parts.name: Dependent
parts.text: The variable that depends on, or is a consequence of, another variable.

parts.name: Extraneous
parts.text: Independent variables left out of the study that may still affect the dependent variable.

parts.name: Control
parts.text: Used to minimise the effect of extraneous variables; measured, but its effect is not hypothesised.

parts.name: Moderator
parts.text: Makes the relationship between the independent and dependent variables stronger or weaker; measured, and its effect is hypothesised.

parts.name: Mediator
parts.text: Explains how two variables are related.

name: Conceptual Model
description: A diagram showing how the variables in a study fit together.

parts.name: Independent to dependent variable
parts.text: The main arrow of the model.

parts.name: Moderating variable
parts.text: Points onto the main arrow and changes the relationship.

parts.name: Mediating variable
parts.text: Sits between the independent and the dependent variable.

parts.name: Control variable
parts.text: Points to the dependent variable.

name: The Research Process
description: Six stages that take a study from a management dilemma to the final report.

parts.name: Stage I: Clarifying the research question
parts.text: Discover the management dilemma, explore reports and previous studies, define the management question, explore through interviews and define the research question.

parts.name: Stage II: Proposing research
parts.text: Allocate resources and budget, value the research information and prepare the research proposal.

parts.name: Stage III: Research methodology
parts.text: Research design, sampling design and a pilot test.

parts.name: Stage IV: Data collection and preparation
parts.text: Primary and secondary data.

parts.name: Stage V: Data analysis and interpretation

name: Hypothesis Testing: The Eight Steps
description: The eight steps used to test a hypothesis and turn the result into a business decision.

parts.name: Step 1
parts.text: Establish a null and alternative hypothesis.

parts.name: Step 2
parts.text: Determine the appropriate statistical test.

parts.name: Step 3
parts.text: Set the value of alpha, the Type I error rate.

parts.name: Step 4
parts.text: Establish the decision rule.

parts.name: Step 5
parts.text: Gather sample data.

parts.name: Step 6
parts.text: Analyze the data.

parts.name: Step 7
parts.text: Reach a statistical conclusion.

parts.name: Step 8
parts.text: Make a business decision.

name: Type I and Type II Errors
description: A decision table comparing the action taken with the true state of nature.

parts.name: Fail to reject a true null
parts.text: Correct decision.

parts.name: Reject a true null
parts.text: Type I error, with probability alpha (α).

parts.name: Fail to reject a false null
parts.text: Type II error (β).

parts.name: Reject a false null
parts.text: Correct decision (power).

name: Two-tailed and One-tailed Tests
description: Two ways to place the rejection region, depending on the alternative hypothesis.

parts.name: Two-tailed (non-directional)
parts.text: Ha: parameter ≠ value. The rejection region is split between both tails; used when any deviation from the value matters.

parts.name: One-tailed (directional)
parts.text: Ha: parameter > value or parameter < value. The whole rejection region sits in one tail; used when the direction of the effect matters.

name: Common Parametric Tests
description: Parametric tests assume things about the population's parameters and distribution, usually normal.

parts.name: t-tests
parts.text: One-sample, independent two-sample and paired t-tests.

parts.name: Z-test
parts.text: Often for large samples with a known population standard deviation.

parts.name: ANOVA (Analysis of Variance)
parts.text: Compares means across three or more groups (one-way, two-way).

parts.name: Pearson's correlation (r)
parts.text: Measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

name: Types of t-Tests
description: Three t-tests and when each is used.

parts.name: One-sample t-test
parts.text: Compares the mean of one group to a known or hypothesised population mean.

parts.name: Independent two-sample t-test (unpaired)
parts.text: Compares the means of two unrelated groups, such as treatment vs control.

parts.name: Paired (dependent) t-test
parts.text: Compares means from the same group at different times, or matched pairs.

name: Parametric vs. Non-Parametric Tests
description: The two families of tests compared on six points.

parts.name: Data type
parts.text: Parametric: interval or ratio (continuous). Non-parametric: ordinal or nominal.

parts.name: Distribution
parts.text: Parametric: assumes normality. Non-parametric: no assumption of distribution.

parts.name: Measure
parts.text: Parametric: mean and SD. Non-parametric: medians and ranks.

parts.name: Example tests
parts.text: Parametric: t-test, ANOVA, regression. Non-parametric: chi-square, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis.

parts.name: Sample size
parts.text: Parametric: usually large. Non-parametric: works with small samples.

parts.name: Use when
parts.text: Parametric: data is symmetric and continuous. Non-parametric: data is skewed or categorical.

name: Key Non-Parametric Tests
description: Four non-parametric tests, when each is used and a business use.

parts.name: Chi-square
parts.text: Categorical: compares observed with expected frequencies. Use: market share, preference counts.

parts.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank
parts.text: Dependent (paired): compares medians of matched data. Use: pre and post customer feedback.

parts.name: Mann-Whitney U
parts.text: Independent: tests differences between two independent groups. Use: comparing supplier ratings.

parts.name: Kruskal-Wallis
parts.text: Multiple groups: compares three or more independent groups. Use: customer satisfaction across regions.

name: Univariate and Multivariate ANOVA
description: How the number of independent and dependent variables names the kind of ANOVA.

parts.name: One dependent variable
parts.text: Univariate: one-way with 1 IV, two-way with 2 IVs, multi-way with more than 1 IV.

parts.name: More than one dependent variable
parts.text: Multivariate: one-way with 1 IV, two-way with 2 IVs, multi-way with more than 1 IV.

name: Entrepreneurship: Mindset, Skill, Behaviour
description: The opening slide presents entrepreneurship as three things at once.

name: Entrepreneurship & Innovation: Two Kinds of Enterprise
description: Entrepreneurship branches into two kinds of enterprise that grow in different ways.

parts.name: Small business enterprises
parts.text: Serve local markets and grow.

parts.name: Innovation driven enterprises
parts.text: Scale.

name: Small Business vs Entrepreneurial Venture (Wickham, 2006)
description: A diagram with two axes, growth potential and innovation, plus strategic objectives along the bottom. The small business fills a small region near the corner; the entrepreneurial venture covers the much larger outer region.

parts.name: Small business
parts.text: Sits near the corner: lower growth potential, innovation and strategic objectives.

parts.name: Entrepreneurial venture
parts.text: The much larger outer region: higher growth potential, innovation and strategic objectives.

name: Growing versus Scaling
description: Two charts of revenues and costs that show the difference between growing a business and scaling it.

parts.name: Growing
parts.text: Revenues and costs both rise steeply, so costs stay fairly close below revenues.

parts.name: Scaling
parts.text: Revenues rise steeply while costs rise only slowly, so the gap between them widens.

name: Entrepreneurship as a Process of Discovery, Evaluation and Exploitation of Opportunities
description: Entrepreneurship is a process of discovery, evaluation and exploitation of opportunities. The slides walk through it with a fresh vegetables venture.

parts.name: Discovery (existence of need)
parts.text: A need found through customer feedback and self experience: people want fresh vegetables, but vegetables have a short shelf life.

parts.name: Evaluation
parts.text: Are people ready to pay more, and what will maintenance cost?

parts.name: Exploitation
parts.text: Processed vegetables using technology, packed and hygienic, sold at a higher price for profit and less loss.

name: Entrepreneurship = Discovery & Learning
description: Two timelines of venture activity: ventures that emerged and ventures that did not.

parts.name: Emerged
parts.text: High rate, low concentration and late timing of activities.

parts.name: Non-emergent
parts.text: Low rate, high concentration and early timing of activities.

name: Entrepreneurship as a Process of Value Creation
description: Three opportunity stages sit inside a large value creation arrow, fed by four kinds of capital.

parts.name: Four kinds of capital
parts.text: Strategic, economic, cultural and social capital feed all three stages.

name: Types of Entrepreneurship
description: Four types of venture listed on the slide.

name: Commercial Entrepreneurship
description: Entrepreneurship branches into commercial and social entrepreneurship. In commercial entrepreneurship, economic value creation comes first and social value is a byproduct.

parts.name: Economic value creation
parts.text: Leads to profit and wealth creation, and to negative externalities.

parts.name: Social value is a byproduct
parts.text: Through CSR, employment and taxes.

name: Social Entrepreneurship
description: In social entrepreneurship, social value creation comes first, and economic value is a necessity.

parts.name: Social value creation
parts.text: Filling institutional voids and overcoming market failures.

parts.name: Economic value is a necessity
parts.text: For the sustainability of the social enterprise.

name: Marks of Social Entrepreneurship
description: Four features that set social entrepreneurship apart.

parts.name: Social purpose
parts.text: Embedded in the organization's DNA.

parts.name: Neglected problems
parts.text: Targets neglected social problems.

parts.name: Value capture
parts.text: The potential for value capture is less than the potential for value creation.

parts.name: Positive externalities
parts.text: Internalized costs are more, and externalized benefits are more.

name: Social Enterprise Continuum
description: Seven kinds of organization, from a charity that relies on grants to a commercial enterprise. The four circles in the middle are shaded on the slide.

parts.name: Charity relying on fundraising or grant income
Trading company providing at least 51% of profits to charity
Enterprise delivering benefits to people and communities
Enterprise delivering high levels of social impact
Business run in a socially responsible way

name: Continuum of Social Entrepreneurs in Six Descending Degrees of Altruism
description: Six kinds of social entrepreneur, from the most self-sacrificing to the most self-interested.

parts.name: Degree 1
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit society alone, at risk of personal loss: a creative philanthropist willing to martyr self for others.

parts.name: Degree 2
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit society alone, at risk of forgoing personal profit.

parts.name: Degree 3
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit society by profiting himself, at risk of personal loss.

parts.name: Degree 4
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit society by profiting himself, at risk of forgoing personal profit.

parts.name: Degree 5
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit himself by profiting society, at risk of personal loss.

parts.name: Degree 6
parts.text: Tries to innovatively profit himself by profiting society, at risk of forgoing personal profit.

name: Social Enterprise Continuum (CAF Venturesome)
description: Eight kinds of organization from pure commercial enterprise to operational charity. Impact investing spans the six middle boxes, and returns are blended across the range.

parts.name: Business giving a portion of profits to charity
On-mission enterprising arm of a charity

name: Social Entrepreneurship Continuum: Four Types
description: Four types of social enterprise, each shown with an example.

parts.name: Community-based enterprises
parts.text: Charitable organizations carrying out social goals that involve risk, bridging gaps in services. Example: Grace Orchard School in Singapore.

parts.name: Socially responsible enterprises
parts.text: Example: Banyan Tree Gallery, an extension of the social consciousness of Banyan Tree Holiday Resorts.

parts.name: Social service industry professionals
parts.text: Example: Northern Leaf Communications, a PR firm that couples its business objective with its non-profit clients' social goals.

parts.name: Socio-economic or dualistic enterprises
parts.text: Have the dual objective of earning profits and running non-profit activities for the community. Example: Transnational Recycling Industries.

name: 3 Types of Legal Structures for Hybrids
description: Legal forms for hybrid organizations, which pursue a social mission but rely on commercial revenue. Program-related investments (PRIs) also let private foundations fund hybrids.

parts.name: L3C (Low Profit Ltd Liability)
parts.text: A variant of an LLC, designed to attract investment from tax-exempt sources such as private foundations.

parts.name: Benefit Corporation
parts.text: Considers a designated social purpose and its social impact alongside financial analysis when making business decisions.

parts.name: Flexible Purpose Corporation
parts.text: Requires boards and management to agree with shareholders on one or more social and environmental purposes. In Washington it is called the Social Purpose Corporation.

name: The MBA Entrepreneurship Model
description: Every student team must launch an asset-light, high-margin, knowledge-based business and take it through six stages.

parts.name: Stage 1
parts.text: Form the team and delegate operations.

parts.name: Stage 2
parts.text: Document business ideation meetings, metrics and outcomes.

parts.name: Stage 3
parts.text: Create SOPs.

parts.name: Stage 4
parts.text: Acquire the first customer.

parts.name: Stage 5
parts.text: Generate the first revenue.

parts.name: Stage 6
parts.text: Increase revenue.

name: Startup Pitching Template (Very Early Stage)
description: The sections of a very early stage startup pitch, in order.

parts.name: Startup name
parts.text: What you aspire to do, in the most interesting manner.

parts.name: Problem statement
parts.text: The problem you intend to solve.

parts.name: Solution
parts.text: Unique feature, significant advantage, major benefit, value proposition, and what is new compared with what people are forced to do now.

parts.name: Market size
parts.text: Total available market, and the target market at the first stage.

parts.name: Customer segments
parts.text: Key characteristics, pain points and goals of the segments you serve.

parts.name: Insight
parts.text: What you understand that others just don't know.

parts.name: Uniqueness or unfair advantage
parts.text: Why it would be hard for others to duplicate what you do.

parts.name: Business unit economics
parts.text: Average cost per transaction and average revenue per transaction.

parts.name: Revenue streams
parts.text: How you will make money: strategies such as pay-per-use, subscription or licensing, not revenue projections.

parts.name: Team competency
parts.text: Why you are best suited to solve the problem: qualification, professional experience and something interesting about the team.

parts.name: Scalability
parts.text: When, where, and how (the promotion plan).

parts.name: Requirement
parts.text: How much you need, and for what purpose.

parts.name: Exit
parts.text: When, and for how much.
